confirmed: 266 participants completed the study. The 43 who failed the attention check were 'excluded from further analysis, leaving a final sample of 225'. The abstract also gives 225 university students. (p. 4, Section 2.1; p. 1, Abstract)

The group counts are 58, 60, 54 and 53 people. They sum to 225, and the printed shares (26, 27, 24 and 24 percent) fit 225. The 107 participants with prior ChatGPT experience equal Groups 3 + 4 (54 + 53). (p. 4, Section 2.2)
266 - 43 = 223, not 225. The form flags this in participants.exclusions, the eligibility reason and open_questions. (p. 4, Section 2.1)

The p. 8 tests print t(221) twice, for a within-person comparison (moral acceptance with vs without transparency), and t(220) for Control vs AI. Both imply 222 people. The form reports these df but does not state the implied 222. (p. 8, Section 3.3)
No creativity analysis prints its N or df. The pooled regressions are in SI Table 3, which is not in this PDF. (pp. 5-6, Section 3.2)

Random assignment covered 'all participants', between subjects, after the pre-task survey. The 43 excluded people had completed the study, so they went through assignment. At least 266 people were randomized, and the paper reports no count of people who started but did not finish, so n_randomized = null is correct for an exact count. (p. 4, Fig. 1 caption and Section 2.1; p. 5, Section 2.2)
No arm sizes appear in the text or in Figs. 1-6, so the null arm counts are correct. The paper describes SI Table 1 only as a detailed demographic breakdown. (pp. 4-10; p. 4, Section 2.2)

Comprehension checks removed no one: participants who failed were reminded and had to answer correctly before going on. The four subgroups dropped for small size are cells of the heterogeneity analysis (Fig. 3), not people removed from the sample. (p. 5, Section 2.2; p. 6, Section 3.2.1)

All counts in participants and arms are people ('participants', 'Forty-three people', 'n = 58'). The 40 validation items are responses (5 per group and condition). The Fig. 5 values (552, 635, 313, 442) are counts of uses and domains, which the form codes as outcomes with unit 'set'. (p. 4; p. 5, Section 2.3; p. 9, Fig. 5)

The 'who' field matches the PDF: current UK university students recruited via Prolific, mean age 29.07 (SD 8.59), 51 percent male, 48 percent female, 60 percent undergraduates, 31 percent postgraduates including 13 PhD students. (p. 4, Section 2.1)

The paper reports one experiment. The heterogeneity, HAI-dyad, group-level and perception analyses reuse its participants. The paper names no other paper on this sample. No other screening candidate shares its authors or the printer task, and the University of Bath portal page for the GW4 project (4982.50) lists no outputs. (whole PDF; candidates.json; researchportal.bath.ac.uk)
Criterion 2 holds under every count the paper prints: 225, 223 or 222 people analyzed, all far above 50. (p. 4; p. 8)
summary: Every participant count in the form matches the PDF: 266 completed, 43 excluded, a stated final sample of 225 (p. 4 and abstract), four groups of 58, 60, 54 and 53 people, and no arm sizes anywhere in the text or Figs. 1-6, so the null arm counts are right and criterion 2 holds by a wide margin. The form already flags that 266 - 43 = 223, and it could add that the p. 8 tests (df 221 within subjects, df 220 between arms) imply 222 people and that the 43 excluded had completed the study, so at least 266 people were randomized.
